body:
FPIs allocate top-down. India's weight in MSCI EM fell from about 19–20% in late 2024 to about 12% by April 2026, as AI-chip-heavy Taiwan and Korea rallied. Combined with a still-high valuation premium, rupee weakness (about 96–97 per USD in Oct 2026) and soft earnings, this produced record outflows:
- about ₹1.66 lakh crore in 2025;
- about ₹2.45 lakh crore by Sept 2026.

Record SIP-fed domestic buying absorbed the selling. SEBI recorded ₹8.5 lakh crore of net DII inflow in FY26, and monthly SIPs were about ₹31–32k crore in 2026.

`event:india-covid-crash-2020` | confidence: **verified** | tags: india, base-rate, smallcap, policy, rerating

Nifty ~12,430 (Jan 2020 high; 12,168 cited as the pre-crash reference) to 7,511 on 24 Mar 2020, about -38 to -40%; Sensex ~42,270 to ~25,640 (levels from memory). Nifty 50 TRI -38% vs Smallcap 250 TRI -43% (DSP); Smallcap 100 intra-year fall -47%. Market cap/GDP fell to ~56% in March 2020 (Business Standard; other estimates ~70% on FY20 GDP) - the lowest in a decade. Recovery: the Nifty regained its high in Nov 2020 (about 8-10 months; sources differ on day counts), doubled to 15,000 by Feb 2021, and the Smallcap 100 was up 141% from its March low by the end of FY21. Bottom signals: global central-bank 'whatever it takes' (Fed unlimited QE 23 Mar 2020; RBI's 75bp cut on 27 Mar), valuation near decade lows, forced selling and record pessimism, a surge in new retail demat accounts. Leaders of the recovery: pharma, IT, specialty chemicals, metals, then small caps broadly; laggards: banks (loan moratorium), hotels, aviation. Rs 1 lakh in Smallcap 250 TRI at the Mar 2020 bottom became ~Rs 5 lakh by Mar 2026 (~31% CAGR) vs ~Rs 2.9 lakh (~19%) if invested in Jan 2020 (DSP). Lesson: exogenous crashes met by massive liquidity recover fastest; the best entries came when valuation indicators (mcap/GDP <60-70%) and policy turned together.

| key | value |
|---|---|
| peak | Nifty ~12,430 (Jan 2020) |
| trough | 7,511 (24 Mar 2020) |
| drawdown | ~-38 to -40% (Nifty); SC250 TRI -43% |
| mcap_gdp_trough | ~56% |
| recovery | ~8-10 months |
| lesson | liquidity + cheap valuation = fast recovery |

`person:group-gmr` · flag: **mixed** · confidence: single-source · tickers: GMRAIRPORT, GMRP&UI

Flag: MIXED. Airports-energy-infrastructure group (Delhi and Hyderabad airports; Goa, overseas airports). Survived a 2013-2020 leverage crisis via asset sales and strategic equity (Tata-GIC-SSG 2019 deal, Groupe ADP buying 49% of GMR Airports Ltd for ~Rs 10,780 cr in 2020). Restructuring: 2021 demerger of non-airport businesses (energy, urban infra, EPC) into GMR Power & Urban Infra (GPUIL), leaving GMR Airports Infrastructure (GIL) as an airport pure-play; 2024 merger of GIL with unlisted GMR Airports Ltd to simplify the structure and settle most GPUIL-related contingent liabilities. Minority concerns: long history of the listed holdco supporting loss-making energy subsidiaries through loans/guarantees; complex multi-layer structure with holdco discount; persistently high promoter encumbrance -- an aggregator summary of a Nov-2025 filing put ~50.6% of promoter shares in GPUIL as encumbered (verify on NSE SAST). No SEBI/ED fraud findings against the promoters were found in this scan; the Maldives airport cancellation (2012) and Indonesian coal assets were capital-allocation losses. Positives: airport-business value has been preserved and grown; strategic partners came in at arm's length prices; promoter has not been accused of siphoning. Status Nov-2026: GIL is the main listed vehicle; watch encumbrance, RPT approvals between GPUIL and GIL, and dilution via preferential/ convertible issues to partners.

- **red flags:** high encumbrance at GPUIL; inter-group support for energy losses; layered holdcos
- **good conduct:** demerger 2021; merger 2024 simplification; strategic equity at arm's length

**Data.** 20-F FY2025 (0001575872-25-000393), ₹ million. Shares are split-adjusted (1:5 split in 2024).

| Test (1 point each) | Computation | Point |
|---|---|---|
| 1. ROA > 0 | NI 57,245 / opening TA 387,518 = 14.8% | 1 |
| 2. CFO > 0 | 46,428 | 1 |
| 3. ΔROA > 0 | 14.8% vs FY24 55,684/321,854 = 17.3% | 0 |
| 4. CFO/TA > ROA (accrual) | 12.0% < 14.8% | 0 |
| 5. ΔLeverage (LTD/avg TA) falls | 1.79% vs 1.69% | 0 |
| 6. ΔCurrent ratio > 0 | 250,112/130,392 = 1.92 vs 2.58 | 0 |
| 7. No new shares | 832.6 m vs 830.8 m (ESOPs) | 0 |
| 8. ΔGross margin > 0 | 58.50% vs 58.61% | 0 |
| 9. ΔAsset turnover > 0 | 0.840 vs 0.867 | 0 |
| **F-score** | | **2 / 9** |

- **Why a high-quality company scores 2.** In FY25 Dr. Reddy's bought Haleon's Nicotinell NRT portfolio for £458 m upfront (completed 30-Sep-2024). The deal was funded partly with short-term borrowings: proceeds from borrowings were ₹80,646 m against ₹19,366 m the year before.
- Total assets jumped 27%, so asset turnover, the current ratio and ROA all fell mechanically.
- Piotroski designed F for **cheap, high book-to-market** stocks (value traps vs recoveries). On a growth or quality company, in an acquisition year, it misfires.
- **Rules:**
  - (a) Use F only on the cheapest book-to-market quintile, as Piotroski did. His high-F minus low-F spread was about 23% a year in 1976–96.
  - (b) Re-run it excluding acquisitions (pro-forma assets).
  - (c) Treat 8–9 as "improving fundamentals", ≤ 2 as "deteriorating", and check *why* before acting.
- The strict share test (7) fails on tiny ESOP issuance. Some practitioners allow under 1% dilution.
